hld-storage-observability:0.prompt: Users upload 200 MB videos. Why is a presigned S3 PUT URL usually better than streaming the upload through your Node.js API server?
options: Presigned URLs compress the file automatically
The client uploads directly to object storage, so large bytes never tie up your API servers' bandwidth, memory and connections
S3 rejects uploads that pass through an application server
Presigned URLs make the object publicly readable forever
hld-storage-observability:0.explanation: Direct-to-storage uploads offload the heavy transfer to S3, which scales for it, while your API only issues a short-lived signed URL. They do not compress anything, and a presigned PUT grants upload permission, not public read access.

hld-storage-observability:0.prompt: What does a presigned URL actually contain that authorises the request?
options: Your AWS secret access key in plain text
A session cookie for the user
A signature computed with the issuer's credentials over the method, bucket/key, expiry and other parameters, which S3 verifies
A one-time password emailed to the user
hld-storage-observability:0.explanation: The URL carries the access key id, expiry and an HMAC-based signature (SigV4) over the request details; S3 recomputes and checks it. The secret key itself is never included, and changing the method or key invalidates the signature.

hld-storage-observability:0.prompt: A presigned download URL for a private invoice leaks in a support chat. What property limits the damage most?
options: Bucket versioning
Server-side encryption with S3-managed keys
Cross-region replication
A short expiry on the presigned URL (e.g. minutes), after which it no longer works
hld-storage-observability:0.explanation: Anyone with a valid presigned URL can use it until it expires, so short expiries bound exposure. Server-side encryption protects data at rest but S3 decrypts it transparently for any authorised request, including a leaked presigned URL.

hld-storage-observability:0.prompt: After a client uploads to a presigned URL, how should your backend learn the upload finished and is valid?
options: Trust the client's 'upload done' call without checking anything
Poll the bucket listing every second
Use a storage event notification (or have the client confirm and the server HEAD the object) and then validate size/type before marking it usable
Assume success once the presigned URL was issued
hld-storage-observability:0.explanation: Issuing a URL does not mean an upload happened. Event notifications (e.g. S3 to SQS/Lambda) or a confirm-then-HEAD check, followed by validation (and malware scanning if needed), are reliable. Bucket listing polls are slow and costly.

hld-storage-observability:0.prompt: Uploads of multi-GB files over mobile networks often fail near the end and restart from zero. What should you use?
options: Multipart upload: split into parts uploaded (and retried) independently, then complete the upload to assemble them
A longer expiry on a single presigned PUT
Base64-encode the file before uploading
Upload through a WebSocket to your API
hld-storage-observability:0.explanation: S3 multipart upload lets parts upload in parallel and retry individually, then a CompleteMultipartUpload call stitches them together (each part can get its own presigned URL). A longer expiry does not fix restarting from zero, and base64 inflates size by about 33%.

hld-storage-observability:0.prompt: Why is object storage like S3 a poor fit as the primary store for a frequently updated user-profile record?
options: Objects cannot exceed 1 MB
S3 does not support HTTPS
Object storage has no notion of keys
Objects are replaced whole on every write (no partial updates or queries on fields), and per-request latency is higher than a database
hld-storage-observability:0.explanation: Object stores are optimised for large immutable blobs: you PUT the whole object, cannot query by field, and pay tens of ms per request. Small mutable, queryable records belong in a database. S3 objects can be up to 5 TB.

hld-storage-observability:0.prompt: A presigned PUT URL is issued for key `avatars/123.png` with no constraints. What abuse is possible?
options: The client can delete the whole bucket
The client can upload any content of any size (e.g. a 5 GB file or HTML instead of an image) to that key until the URL expires
The client can read every object in the bucket
The client can change the bucket policy
hld-storage-observability:0.explanation: A presigned PUT allows exactly one operation on one key, but without constraints the content is unchecked. Use a presigned POST policy with content-length-range and content-type conditions, short expiries, and server-side validation after upload.

hld-storage-observability:0.prompt: Which are good practices for serving user-uploaded files from object storage? Select all that apply.
options: Keep the bucket private and issue short-lived presigned GET URLs (or use a CDN with signed URLs/cookies)
Use random or unguessable object keys rather than sequential ids
Serve files from a separate domain to avoid uploaded HTML/JS running on your main app origin
Make the bucket public-read so the CDN can cache everything
Set lifecycle rules to delete abandoned incomplete multipart uploads
hld-storage-observability:0.explanation: Private buckets with signed access, unguessable keys, a separate serving domain and lifecycle cleanup are standard. Public-read buckets expose all private uploads; a CDN can use origin access control to read a private bucket instead.

hld-storage-observability:0.prompt: Which statements about Amazon S3 are correct today? Select all that apply.
options: S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for PUTs and DELETEs of objects
A single object can be up to 5 TB
S3 supports appending bytes to the middle of an existing standard object in place
Storage classes (e.g. Standard, Infrequent Access, Glacier) trade retrieval cost/latency for cheaper storage
hld-storage-observability:0.explanation: Since December 2020, S3 is strongly consistent for object reads after writes; objects can be 5 TB; storage classes trade access cost for storage cost. Standard objects are immutable, so you cannot edit bytes in place; you rewrite the object.

hld-storage-observability:0.prompt: A presigned URL can grant more permission than the IAM identity that signed it has.
options: True
False
hld-storage-observability:0.explanation: False. A presigned URL acts with the signer's permissions; if the signer lacks access (or its temporary credentials expire), the URL fails even before its own expiry. Sign with a narrowly scoped role.

hld-storage-observability:0.prompt: Putting a CDN in front of object storage reduces latency for globally distributed users and cuts egress requests to the bucket for popular files.
options: True
False
hld-storage-observability:0.explanation: True. Edge caches serve repeat requests close to users, so the origin bucket sees only cache misses. Private content can still be protected with signed URLs or cookies at the CDN.

hld-storage-observability:1.prompt: What is an inverted index in Elasticsearch?
options: A B-tree on the document id sorted in descending order
A map from each term to the list of documents (and positions) that contain it
A copy of the index stored in reverse byte order
A cache of the most recent queries
hld-storage-observability:1.explanation: Lucene, under Elasticsearch, maps terms to posting lists of document ids, so finding documents containing 'timeout' is a lookup rather than a scan. That is why full-text search is fast where a SQL LIKE '%timeout%' scans every row.

hld-storage-observability:1.prompt: A product search for 'Running Shoes' must match a document containing 'running shoe'. Which Elasticsearch feature makes this work?
options: Index replicas
Shard routing
Analyzers: tokenising and normalising text (lowercasing, stemming) at index time and query time
Doc values
hld-storage-observability:1.explanation: An analyzer splits text into tokens and applies filters like lowercase and stemming, so both sides normalise to 'run' and 'shoe'. Replicas and routing are about distribution; doc values are a column store for sorting and aggregations.

hld-storage-observability:1.prompt: In Elasticsearch, what is the difference between `text` and `keyword` field types?
options: `text` is analysed into tokens for full-text search; `keyword` stores the exact value for filtering, sorting and aggregations
`keyword` is analysed; `text` is stored exactly
`text` fields are limited to 256 characters
They are the same type with different names
hld-storage-observability:1.explanation: Use `text` for search over prose and `keyword` for exact matches like status codes, ids or tags, and for terms aggregations. A term query on an analysed `text` field often surprises people because the stored tokens are lowercased/split.

hld-storage-observability:1.prompt: Why can't you change the number of primary shards of an existing Elasticsearch index in place?
options: Shards are stored on separate clusters
Primary shard count is limited to 1 for indexes over 1 GB
Replica count also cannot be changed
Documents are routed to a primary shard by hash(routing) mod number_of_primary_shards, so changing the count would invalidate every document's location
hld-storage-observability:1.explanation: Routing depends on the shard count, so changing it needs a reindex (or the split/shrink APIs, which create a new index). Replica count, by contrast, can be changed at any time.

hld-storage-observability:1.prompt: A document is indexed successfully, but an immediate search does not return it. A second later it appears. Why?
options: Elasticsearch search is near real-time: new documents become searchable after a refresh (default every 1 s) creates a new segment
The replica shard rejected the write
The document was routed to the wrong shard at first
The analyzer runs asynchronously once per minute
hld-storage-observability:1.explanation: Indexed documents are written to a buffer and become visible to search at the next refresh (default 1 second for indexes that are being searched). A GET by id can still read it immediately. You can force refresh=wait_for on writes, at a throughput cost.

hld-storage-observability:1.prompt: A team creates a new index per day with 5 primaries and 1 replica, keeping 2 years of small log indexes. The cluster becomes slow and unstable. What is the most likely cause?
options: Too few replicas
Oversharding: thousands of tiny shards, each with fixed memory and cluster-state overhead
The inverted index is too large
Daily indexes are not supported
hld-storage-observability:1.explanation: 730 indexes × 10 shards = 7,300 shards, mostly tiny. Each shard has overhead on the master and data nodes. Use fewer primaries, rollover by size (e.g. tens of GB per shard via ILM) and delete or shrink old data.

hld-storage-observability:1.prompt: Why is Elasticsearch usually NOT used as the primary system of record for orders, with the database as the source of truth instead?
options: Elasticsearch cannot store JSON documents
Elasticsearch has no replication
It lacks multi-document ACID transactions and is near real-time, so it is better as a derived index rebuilt from the source of truth
Elasticsearch cannot handle more than 1 million documents
hld-storage-observability:1.explanation: Search indexes are optimised for querying, not transactional integrity: no multi-document transactions, refresh delays and mapping changes that need reindexing. Keep the database authoritative and sync to Elasticsearch via CDC or events so you can rebuild it.

hld-storage-observability:1.prompt: How do replica shards help an Elasticsearch cluster? Select all that apply.
options: They provide failover if a node holding the primary is lost
They can serve search requests, increasing read throughput
They increase write throughput because writes go only to replicas
They let you increase the primary shard count later
hld-storage-observability:1.explanation: Replicas give redundancy and spread search load. Writes go to the primary and are then replicated, so replicas add write work rather than reducing it, and they have nothing to do with changing the primary count.

hld-storage-observability:1.prompt: You keep a PostgreSQL products table in sync with an Elasticsearch index. Which approaches are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Change data capture (e.g. Debezium reading the WAL) streaming changes to an indexer
Transactional outbox events consumed by an indexer that upserts by product id
Dual writes from the API: write PostgreSQL, then Elasticsearch, with no retry or reconciliation
Periodic full reindex into a new index plus alias swap to repair drift
Use external versioning (e.g. the row's updated version) so out-of-order updates don't overwrite newer data
hld-storage-observability:1.explanation: CDC or outbox give reliable change streams; versioned upserts handle reordering; alias-swapped reindexes repair drift with zero downtime. Unprotected dual writes leave the two stores inconsistent whenever the second write fails.

hld-storage-observability:1.prompt: Deep pagination with `from` + `size` (e.g. page 10,000) is cheap in Elasticsearch because each shard returns only the requested page.
options: True
False
hld-storage-observability:1.explanation: False. Each shard must collect from + size top hits and the coordinator merges them all, so cost grows with depth; index.max_result_window defaults to 10,000. Use search_after (with a point-in-time) for deep paging.

hld-storage-observability:1.prompt: Elasticsearch ranks full-text matches by default using BM25 relevance scoring.
options: True
False
hld-storage-observability:1.explanation: True. Since Elasticsearch 5, the default similarity is BM25, which considers term frequency (with saturation), inverse document frequency and field length. Plain TF-IDF was the older default.

hld-storage-observability:2.prompt: Which workload is a typical OLTP workload?
options: Monthly revenue by region over 3 years of data
Training a churn model on all customer history
A checkout flow inserting an order and updating stock for one customer in milliseconds
A dashboard of average session length per country
hld-storage-observability:2.explanation: OLTP is many small, short transactions touching few rows with low latency. The other options scan and aggregate large data volumes, which is OLAP territory.

hld-storage-observability:2.prompt: Why are columnar stores (e.g. BigQuery, Redshift, ClickHouse) faster for analytical queries like SUM(amount) GROUP BY country over billions of rows?
options: They keep all data in RAM
They store each column contiguously, so a query reads only the columns it needs and compresses them very well
They use B-tree indexes on every column
They enforce foreign keys more efficiently
hld-storage-observability:2.explanation: Reading 2 of 50 columns means scanning a fraction of the bytes, and same-typed column data compresses and vectorises well. Row stores must read whole rows. Columnar warehouses usually avoid per-row B-tree indexes rather than adding them everywhere.

hld-storage-observability:2.prompt: Analysts run heavy reporting queries directly on the production PostgreSQL primary, and checkout latency spikes every morning. What is the best long-term fix?
options: Move analytics to a separate store (a read replica short-term, a data warehouse fed by CDC/ETL long-term)
Add more indexes to every table
Run reports at noon instead
Increase max_connections
hld-storage-observability:2.explanation: Isolating analytical load protects OLTP latency; a warehouse also suits large scans with columnar storage. More indexes slow writes and don't fix big scans, and more connections increase contention.

hld-storage-observability:2.prompt: In a star schema, what are fact and dimension tables?
options: Facts are lookup tables; dimensions are event tables
Facts hold measurable events (e.g. order lines with amount, quantity) with keys to dimensions; dimensions hold descriptive attributes (customer, product, date)
Facts hold only aggregates; dimensions hold raw logs
Both are fully normalised to 3NF to save space
hld-storage-observability:2.explanation: A central fact table of events references denormalised dimension tables used to filter and group. Star schemas deliberately denormalise dimensions for simpler, faster analytical joins, unlike 3NF OLTP design.

hld-storage-observability:2.prompt: What is the main difference between ETL and ELT?
options: ETL is for streaming; ELT is only batch
ELT cannot handle JSON
ETL loads directly into OLTP databases only
ETL transforms data before loading into the warehouse; ELT loads raw data first and transforms inside the warehouse (e.g. with SQL/dbt)
hld-storage-observability:2.explanation: Modern cloud warehouses are powerful enough to transform in place, so ELT keeps raw data and makes transformations reproducible SQL. ETL transforms in a separate engine before loading. Both can be batch or near-real-time.

hld-storage-observability:2.prompt: Why do OLTP schemas tend to be normalised while warehouse schemas are often denormalised?
options: Warehouses don't support joins
Normalisation avoids update anomalies for frequent small writes; warehouses are mostly append/read-heavy, so denormalising cuts expensive joins over huge scans
Normalised schemas use more disk
Denormalised schemas are required for ACID
hld-storage-observability:2.explanation: OLTP writes constantly, so storing each fact once keeps updates consistent. Analytical data is loaded in batches and read massively; duplicating attributes trades storage for faster queries. Warehouses do support joins, just at a higher cost at scale.

hld-storage-observability:2.prompt: A product dimension changes a product's category. Analysts need last year's revenue to stay attributed to the old category. Which technique handles this?
options: Overwrite the category in place (SCD Type 1)
Delete the old product row
A Slowly Changing Dimension Type 2: add a new row with a new surrogate key and validity dates, keeping the old row for historical facts
Store the category only in the fact table's JSON
hld-storage-observability:2.explanation: SCD Type 2 versions dimension rows, so old facts keep pointing to the old version while new facts use the new one. Type 1 overwrites history, so last year's revenue would move to the new category.

hld-storage-observability:2.prompt: Which are characteristics of OLAP workloads? Select all that apply.
options: Queries scan and aggregate many rows
High volume of single-row updates with strict millisecond latency
Mostly read-heavy with bulk or streaming loads
Data often lags the source by minutes or hours
Each query touches only a few columns of wide tables
hld-storage-observability:2.explanation: OLAP scans and aggregates, reads more than it writes, accepts some freshness lag and typically touches few columns. Frequent single-row low-latency updates describe OLTP.

hld-storage-observability:2.prompt: A product team wants a real-time dashboard (seconds-fresh) of orders per minute at high scale. Which options are reasonable? Select all that apply.
options: Stream order events (e.g. Kafka) into a real-time OLAP store like ClickHouse or Apache Druid
Run COUNT(*) on the OLTP orders table every second from every dashboard viewer
Maintain pre-aggregated per-minute counters updated by a stream processor
Use a nightly batch ETL into the warehouse
Use a materialised/rollup table in the analytical store refreshed incrementally
hld-storage-observability:2.explanation: Streaming into a real-time OLAP store, stream-processor counters and incremental rollups all give seconds-fresh results without loading OLTP. Polling COUNT(*) per viewer hammers production, and nightly ETL is far too stale.

hld-storage-observability:2.prompt: A PostgreSQL read replica is a full replacement for a data warehouse for large-scale analytics.
options: True
False
hld-storage-observability:2.explanation: False. A replica isolates load from the primary but is still a row store with the OLTP schema, so huge scans and joins stay slow, and long queries can conflict with replication (query cancellation or bloat). It's a stopgap, not a warehouse.

hld-storage-observability:2.prompt: Columnar storage makes updating a single row expensive compared with a row store, which is one reason warehouses favour batch appends.
options: True
False
hld-storage-observability:2.explanation: True. A row's values are spread across many compressed column files, so a point update touches many of them; columnar engines handle updates via deletes plus appends and background merges. Hence batch or append-heavy ingestion.

hld-storage-observability:3.prompt: A Bloom filter says an element is 'possibly present' or 'definitely not present'. What kind of error can it make?
options: False negatives only
False positives only: it may say present when the item was never added
Both false positives and false negatives
No errors, it is exact
hld-storage-observability:3.explanation: Bits are only ever set, never cleared, so an added item always finds its bits set (no false negatives). Other items can set the same bits, giving false positives at a rate that depends on size, hash count and fill.

hld-storage-observability:3.prompt: A URL shortener wants to check whether a randomly generated short code is already taken without querying the database for most new codes. What is a good use of a Bloom filter here?
options: Store all codes in the Bloom filter and skip the database entirely for every check
If the filter says 'definitely not present', accept the code without a DB lookup; if 'possibly present', check the database
Use the Bloom filter to delete expired codes
Use the Bloom filter to count how many times each code is clicked
hld-storage-observability:3.explanation: 'Not present' answers are reliable, so most new codes avoid a DB round-trip; 'maybe' answers fall back to the source of truth. Trusting the filter alone would reject free codes on false positives, and plain Bloom filters can't delete or count.

hld-storage-observability:3.prompt: Why can't you remove an item from a standard Bloom filter?
options: Removal would require rehashing all items
Bloom filters are stored on disk only
Clearing its bits could clear bits shared with other items, creating false negatives
The hash functions are not reversible
hld-storage-observability:3.explanation: Multiple items share bits, so clearing one item's bits can make other items appear absent. Counting Bloom filters (counters instead of bits) or Cuckoo filters support deletion at extra space cost.

hld-storage-observability:3.prompt: Which problem is HyperLogLog designed to solve?
options: Estimating the number of distinct elements (cardinality) using a small, fixed amount of memory
Testing set membership
Estimating the frequency of each item
Sorting a stream of numbers
hld-storage-observability:3.explanation: HyperLogLog estimates cardinality, e.g. unique visitors, with about 0.81% standard error in Redis using at most 12 KB per key. Membership is Bloom filter territory and per-item frequency is Count-Min Sketch territory.

hld-storage-observability:3.prompt: You keep a Redis HyperLogLog of unique visitors per day. How do you get unique visitors for the whole week?
options: Sum the seven daily PFCOUNT results
Average the seven daily counts
It is impossible to combine HyperLogLogs
PFMERGE (or PFCOUNT over all seven keys) to union the sketches, then count
hld-storage-observability:3.explanation: HyperLogLogs merge losslessly into the sketch of the union, so PFCOUNT key1..key7 or PFMERGE gives weekly uniques. Summing daily counts double-counts users who visited on several days.

hld-storage-observability:3.prompt: What does a Count-Min Sketch estimate, and in which direction is its error?
options: Distinct count; it can under- or over-estimate equally
Item frequencies; it never underestimates, but may overestimate due to hash collisions
Set membership; it gives false negatives
Exact top-k items with no error
hld-storage-observability:3.explanation: Each item increments one counter per row; collisions only add counts, and taking the minimum across rows reduces but cannot remove the overestimate. So estimates are always at least the true count.

hld-storage-observability:3.prompt: You need the top 100 most-searched terms in the last hour from a stream of 1 billion searches, with limited memory. Which approach fits best?
options: Store an exact hash map of every term in one process
A HyperLogLog of all terms
A Count-Min Sketch for frequency estimates combined with a min-heap of the current top 100 candidates (per time window)
A Bloom filter of seen terms
hld-storage-observability:3.explanation: CMS gives approximate counts in fixed memory and the heap tracks the current leaders; window by hour (e.g. a sketch per minute bucket). HLL only counts distinct terms and Bloom filters only test membership, and an exact map may not fit for a long-tailed stream.

hld-storage-observability:3.prompt: Which statements about Bloom filter sizing are correct? Select all that apply.
options: For a fixed number of items, more bits lowers the false-positive rate
Inserting far more items than the filter was sized for raises the false-positive rate
There is an optimal number of hash functions for a given bits-per-item ratio; too many or too few raises false positives
Adding more hash functions always lowers the false-positive rate
A filter sized for 1% false positives needs roughly 10 bits per item
hld-storage-observability:3.explanation: False-positive rate depends on bits per item and hash count; the optimum is k ≈ (m/n)·ln 2, and 1% needs about 9.6 bits per item. Beyond the optimum, extra hashes fill the bit array faster and raise false positives.

hld-storage-observability:3.prompt: Which are well-known real uses of these probabilistic structures? Select all that apply.
options: LSM-tree databases (e.g. Cassandra, RocksDB) use Bloom filters to skip SSTables that cannot contain a key
Redis offers PFADD/PFCOUNT for HyperLogLog cardinality estimates
Count-Min Sketch to find heavy hitters (e.g. abusive IPs) in network traffic
HyperLogLog for checking whether a password was in a breach list
Bloom filters for exact billing totals
hld-storage-observability:3.explanation: Bloom filters avoid useless disk reads in LSM stores, Redis ships HLL, and CMS finds heavy hitters. HLL cannot answer membership questions (that is a Bloom filter job), and nothing probabilistic should compute exact billing.

hld-storage-observability:3.prompt: A Bloom filter can give a false negative if two items hash to the same bits.
options: True
False
hld-storage-observability:3.explanation: False. Shared bits cause false positives, not false negatives: once an item is added, its bits stay set, so querying it always returns 'possibly present' (unless you use an unsafe deletion scheme).

hld-storage-observability:3.prompt: The memory used by a HyperLogLog stays roughly constant whether it has counted ten thousand or ten billion distinct items.
options: True
False
hld-storage-observability:3.explanation: True. HLL keeps a fixed number of registers (Redis uses up to 12 KB per key, with a sparse encoding for small sets), so memory does not grow with cardinality; accuracy stays around the same relative error.

hld-storage-observability:4.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes logs, metrics and traces?
options: Metrics are numeric time series aggregated over time; logs are discrete event records; traces follow one request across services as a tree of spans
Logs are for production and metrics are for development
Traces are aggregated logs; metrics are sampled traces
All three are just different names for structured logs
hld-storage-observability:4.explanation: Metrics answer 'how much/how often' cheaply, logs give detailed context for single events, and traces show where time went across service hops. They complement each other, and you often link them via trace ids.

hld-storage-observability:4.prompt: What is the relationship between SLI, SLO and SLA?
options: SLA is the internal target, SLO is the measured value, SLI is the contract
SLI is a measured indicator (e.g. % of successful requests under 300 ms); SLO is the internal target for it (99.9%); SLA is the external contract with consequences if missed
They are synonyms used by different companies
SLO is the penalty, SLA is the indicator, SLI is the target
hld-storage-observability:4.explanation: SLIs are measurements, SLOs are targets for them, and SLAs are customer agreements (usually looser than the SLO) with credits or penalties. Setting SLO tighter than SLA gives a buffer before contractual breaches.

hld-storage-observability:4.prompt: A service has a 99.9% monthly availability SLO. Roughly how much downtime (error budget) does that allow in a 30-day month?
options: About 4.3 minutes
About 7.2 hours
About 43 minutes
About 3.6 days
hld-storage-observability:4.explanation: 30 days × 24 h × 60 min = 43,200 minutes; 0.1% of that is 43.2 minutes. 4.3 minutes would be 99.99%, and 7.2 hours would be 99%.

hld-storage-observability:4.prompt: In OpenTelemetry, how does a trace stay connected when service A calls service B over HTTP?
options: Both services write to the same log file
The collector matches spans by timestamp
B queries A's database for the parent span
A injects trace context (W3C `traceparent` header with trace id and parent span id) into the request, and B extracts it to create child spans
hld-storage-observability:4.explanation: Context propagation carries the trace id and parent span id across process boundaries; instrumentation injects and extracts it. Timestamp matching is unreliable and is not how OTel links spans.

hld-storage-observability:4.prompt: A team adds a `user_id` label to its request-latency Prometheus metric. Memory usage on the metrics backend explodes. Why?
options: High cardinality: each unique label value creates a separate time series, so millions of users means millions of series
Histograms cannot have labels
Prometheus does not support string labels
user_id values are too long to store
hld-storage-observability:4.explanation: Every label combination is a separate series, so unbounded labels like user id or request id multiply series count and memory. Put such ids in logs or trace attributes, and keep metric labels low-cardinality (route, status, region).

hld-storage-observability:4.prompt: Why should latency SLOs usually use percentiles (p95/p99) rather than the average?
options: Averages are harder to compute
Percentiles are always lower than averages
Averages hide the tail: a few very slow requests affect many users' experience but barely move the mean
Prometheus cannot compute averages
hld-storage-observability:4.explanation: A mean of 100 ms can coexist with 1% of requests taking 5 s; p99 exposes that tail. Percentiles are not necessarily lower than averages; for skewed latency, p99 is typically far higher.

hld-storage-observability:4.prompt: You run 20 instances and each reports its own p99 latency. A dashboard averages the 20 p99 values to get the service p99. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; averaging percentiles is correct
Percentiles can't be averaged meaningfully; aggregate the underlying histogram buckets across instances and compute the percentile from the combined distribution
You should take the minimum of the p99s instead
You should use the median of the p99s
hld-storage-observability:4.explanation: The average of per-instance p99s isn't the p99 of all requests, especially with uneven traffic or one slow instance. Sum histogram buckets (e.g. histogram_quantile over sum by (le) in Prometheus) and compute the quantile from that.

hld-storage-observability:4.prompt: Which make logs more useful in a microservices system? Select all that apply.
options: Structured (JSON) logs with consistent field names
Including trace id and span id in each log line to correlate with traces
Logging full request bodies including passwords and card numbers for debugging
Appropriate levels so noisy debug logs can be turned off in production
Centralised log aggregation with retention policies
hld-storage-observability:4.explanation: Structured, correlated, levelled and centralised logs are searchable and joinable with traces. Logging secrets or card data is a security and compliance violation (PCI DSS); redact sensitive fields.

hld-storage-observability:4.prompt: Which practices align with good SLO-based alerting? Select all that apply.
options: Alert on fast error-budget burn rate (e.g. budget would be exhausted in hours), paging a human
Alert on slow burn with a ticket rather than a page
Page whenever any single host's CPU exceeds 70%
Base alerts on user-facing symptoms (errors, latency) rather than every internal cause
Freeze risky launches when the error budget is spent
hld-storage-observability:4.explanation: Burn-rate alerts with page/ticket tiers, symptom-based alerting and budget-driven release policy are core SRE practice. Paging on per-host CPU thresholds is noisy cause-based alerting that often doesn't reflect user impact.

hld-storage-observability:4.prompt: Head-based trace sampling (deciding at the start of a request) can miss rare slow or failed requests, which tail-based sampling at the collector can keep.
options: True
False
hld-storage-observability:4.explanation: True. Head sampling decides before knowing the outcome, so a 1% sample drops 99% of errors too. Tail sampling buffers complete traces and keeps interesting ones (errors, high latency), at the cost of collector memory and complexity.

hld-storage-observability:4.prompt: An SLO of 100% availability is a good goal for most user-facing services.
options: True
False
hld-storage-observability:4.explanation: False. 100% is unachievable (networks, dependencies and user devices fail) and leaves zero error budget, which freezes all change. Pick a target users actually notice, like 99.9%, and spend the remaining budget on shipping.

options: Gradually shifting a small percentage of traffic to the new version
Running two full environments (blue = current, green = new) and switching all traffic to green at once, keeping blue for instant rollback
Deploying only on weekdays (green) and never on weekends (blue)
Rolling pods one by one in place
hld-storage-observability:5.explanation: Blue-green swaps traffic between two complete environments, so rollback is just switching back. Gradual percentage shifting is canary; replacing pods one by one is a rolling update.

hld-storage-observability:5.prompt: A canary release sends 5% of traffic to v2. What should decide whether to proceed to 25%?
options: A fixed timer, regardless of metrics
Whether the build passed unit tests
Comparing the canary's error rate, latency and key business metrics against the baseline, ideally automatically
Developer confidence in the change
hld-storage-observability:5.explanation: A canary is only useful if real production signals decide promotion; automated analysis against the stable version catches regressions tests miss. Timers and test results alone ignore what the canary actually does in production.

hld-storage-observability:5.prompt: Blue-green switch to a new version that renames a database column fails, and rolling back to blue breaks because blue expects the old column. What practice prevents this?
options: Expand/contract migrations: add the new column, deploy code that works with both, migrate data, then remove the old column in a later release
Always deploy schema changes and code together in one step
Never change the schema
Run the migration after rolling back
hld-storage-observability:5.explanation: Backward-compatible (expand/contract) migrations keep the old and new versions both working against the schema, so either can run and rollback is safe. Coupling schema and code in one step is exactly what breaks rollback.

hld-storage-observability:5.prompt: What is the main benefit of feature flags in deployment strategy?
options: They make the code run faster
They remove the need for testing
They replace database migrations
They decouple deploying code from releasing a feature: code ships dark and is turned on (or off) for users without a redeploy
hld-storage-observability:5.explanation: Flags let you merge and deploy incomplete or risky features hidden, release to a cohort, and kill-switch instantly. They add complexity and need cleanup; they don't replace testing or migrations.

hld-storage-observability:5.prompt: In Docker, what is the difference between an image and a container?
options: An image is a running process; a container is the file on disk
An image is a read-only, layered template (filesystem + metadata); a container is a running (or stopped) instance of an image with its own writable layer
They are the same thing
Images run on Linux and containers run on Windows
hld-storage-observability:5.explanation: Images are immutable templates built from a Dockerfile in layers; containers are instances of an image with a thin writable layer and process isolation. Many containers can run from one image.

hld-storage-observability:5.prompt: A Node.js Dockerfile copies the whole repo, then runs `npm ci`. Every code change re-installs all dependencies, making builds slow. What is the fix?
options: Use `npm install` instead of `npm ci`
Add more RAM to the build machine
Copy `package.json` and `package-lock.json` first, run `npm ci`, then copy the rest of the source, so the dependency layer is cached until the lockfile changes
Install dependencies at container start-up instead of build time
hld-storage-observability:5.explanation: Docker caches layers until an input changes; copying everything first invalidates the install layer on every code edit. Ordering lockfile-then-install-then-source keeps that layer cached. Installing at start-up makes containers slow and non-reproducible.

hld-storage-observability:5.prompt: During a Kubernetes rolling update, users see errors because pods receive traffic before the Node.js app has connected to its database. What is missing?
options: A readiness probe that only passes once the app can serve requests
A liveness probe with a very short timeout
A higher replica count
A larger container image
hld-storage-observability:5.explanation: Without readiness, Kubernetes treats the pod as ready once the container starts and sends traffic immediately. A readiness probe holds traffic until the app is ready. An aggressive liveness probe would just restart slow-starting pods.

hld-storage-observability:5.prompt: Which Kubernetes objects are correctly described? Select all that apply.
options: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets to keep a desired number of identical pods and performs rolling updates
A Service gives a stable network endpoint that load-balances across matching pods
A Pod is the smallest deployable unit, one or more containers sharing network and storage
A ConfigMap stores encrypted secrets by default
A HorizontalPodAutoscaler adjusts replica counts based on metrics such as CPU
hld-storage-observability:5.explanation: Deployments, Services, Pods and HPAs are described correctly. ConfigMaps hold non-secret configuration; Secrets are a separate object, and even they are only base64-encoded unless encryption at rest is configured.

hld-storage-observability:5.prompt: A Node.js app in Kubernetes drops in-flight requests on every deploy. Which changes help achieve graceful shutdown? Select all that apply.
options: Handle SIGTERM: stop accepting new connections, finish in-flight requests, close DB pools, then exit
Fail the readiness probe on SIGTERM so the pod is removed from endpoints
Use a short preStop sleep so endpoint removal propagates before the server stops listening
Run Node under a shell form CMD (`sh -c node server.js`) so the shell handles signals
Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds longer than the longest expected request
hld-storage-observability:5.explanation: Handling SIGTERM, leaving the load-balancer pool first, a preStop delay and a sufficient grace period let in-flight requests finish. A shell-form CMD makes sh PID 1, which typically does not forward SIGTERM to Node, so the app never sees it and gets killed.

hld-storage-observability:5.prompt: Long-lived feature flags that are never removed are harmless because disabled code paths do not run.
options: True
False
hld-storage-observability:5.explanation: False. Stale flags pile up untested combinations, dead code and confusing behaviour; a mistakenly toggled stale flag has caused real outages. Treat release flags as temporary and remove them after full rollout.

hld-storage-observability:5.prompt: Compared with blue-green, a canary release limits the blast radius of a bad version to a small fraction of users, at the cost of running two versions side by side for longer.
options: True
False
hld-storage-observability:5.explanation: True. Canary exposes a few users first and needs both versions (and the schema/APIs) to coexist during the rollout. Blue-green flips everyone at once, which is simpler but means a bad version hits all users until rollback.
